etymology: Hebrew yehoyarib, “the LORD contends” or “whom Jehovah defends,” the head of the first of the four and twenty courses of the priests appointed by David.
biblical_def: Jehoiarib is named as the head of the first course of the priests, the chief upon whom the first lot fell when David, with Zadok and Ahimelech, divided the sons of Aaron into four and twenty orders for the service of the house of God (1Ch 24:7). His name signifies “the LORD contends,” a fitting word for the head of the priestly courses, for the priest stood between a holy God and a sinful people, and the LORD Himself pleaded the cause of His own. The division was not the device of man’s ambition but the ordinance of God through His servant David, that the worship of the sanctuary might be carried on without confusion, each course ministering in its appointed week. The dictionary honours that the LORD is not the author of confusion but of peace, and that He ordered His worship by lot, so that no priest might exalt himself nor any be despised. Jehoiarib, drawing the first lot, led the courses, yet he led them not by his own worthiness but by the providence that ordereth all things. He stands as a witness that the ministry of the old covenant was a shadow of good things to come, pointing beyond all the sons of Aaron to the one great High Priest, the Lord Jesus Christ, who ever liveth to make intercession and contendeth for His people before the throne of God.

biblical_def: Jedaiah is named as the head of the second course of the priests, the chief to whom the second lot came forth when David divided the sons of Aaron into their four and twenty orders for the service of the house of God (1Ch 24:7). His name signifies “the LORD knoweth,” and his course endured even unto the days after the captivity, for among those who returned with Zerubbabel and dwelt at Jerusalem were the priests of the house of Jedaiah (Neh 11:10). Thus the order appointed by David in the first temple was honoured again when the second was built, a witness that the LORD keepeth His ordinances and His servants through the long fall of the ages. The dictionary honours that the worship of God was not left to the whim of each generation, but was ordered by His appointment and preserved by His providence. The priest whose name confessed that the LORD knoweth stood before the God to whom all hearts are open and from whom no secret is hid. Jedaiah stands as a witness that the LORD who knoweth His own ordered the courses that they should serve Him decently and in order, and that the whole priestly ministry, kept through judgment and restoration alike, was a shadow pointing to the High Priest who needeth no successor, even Jesus Christ, who knoweth His sheep and is known of them.

etymology: Hebrew haqqots, “the thorn” or “the nimble,” the head of the seventh of the four and twenty courses of the priests appointed by David.
biblical_def: Hakkoz is named as the head of the seventh course of the priests, the chief to whom the seventh lot came forth when David ordered the sons of Aaron into their courses for the house of the LORD (1Ch 24:10). His name signifies “the thorn,” and a solemn providence attends his house, for in the days of Ezra the children of Koz were among those who sought their register among them that were reckoned by genealogy, and it was not found; therefore were they, as polluted, put from the priesthood (Ezr 2:61-62). The Tirshatha forbade them the most holy things until there stood up a priest with Urim and with Thummim. Yet the LORD did not utterly cast off the house, for Meremoth the son of Urijah the son of Koz wrought faithfully upon the wall under Nehemiah (Neh 3:4,21). The dictionary marks the weight of this: the priesthood of Aaron rested upon a sure register, and he that could not prove his descent might not minister at the altar. There is a sober gospel here, for our acceptance before God rests not upon a genealogy we cannot keep, but upon the High Priest after the order of Melchisedec, who is made priest, not after the law of a carnal commandment, but after the power of an endless life. Hakkoz stands as a witness that the old priesthood was bound to the flesh and could fail, but the priesthood of Christ abideth for ever.

etymology: Hebrew aviyah, “the LORD is my father” or “Jehovah is father,” the head of the eighth of the four and twenty courses of the priests appointed by David.
biblical_def: Abijah is named as the head of the eighth course of the priests, the chief to whom the eighth lot came forth when David divided the sons of Aaron for the service of the house of God (1Ch 24:10). His name signifies “the LORD is my father,” and a singular honour rests upon his course above the rest, for it was of the course of Abia that Zacharias the priest was, who, while he executed the priest’s office before God in the order of his course, beheld the angel Gabriel and received the promise of a son, John the Baptist, the forerunner of the Lord (Luk 1:5). Thus the very ordering of the courses appointed under David, kept through all the ages unto the days of Herod the king, was the appointed frame within which the LORD set forward the coming of His Christ. The dictionary honours that nothing in the worship of God is idle or by chance, for the lot that fell to Abijah a thousand years before placed Zacharias at the altar of incense in the fulness of time. Abijah stands as a witness that the ordered worship of the old covenant, established decently and in order, was no dead form but the very channel through which the dayspring from on high should visit His people; and his course, leading to the father of the Baptist, leads on to the Lamb of God that taketh away the sin of the world.

Huppah, otherwise unknown, served in his station as a minister of that covering which was but a shadow. He stands as a witness that God is not the author of confusion but of order, and that all the covering of the old priesthood pointed to the one perfect covering, even the blood of Christ, under whose canopy the redeemed dwell secure for ever.

etymology: Hebrew yeshev’av, “seat of the father” or “dwelling of the father,” the head of the fourteenth of the four and twenty courses of the priests appointed by David.
biblical_def: Jeshebeab is named as the head of the fourteenth course of the priests, the chief to whom the fourteenth lot came forth when David ordered the sons of Aaron into their courses for the ministry of the house of the LORD (1Ch 24:13). His name signifies “seat of the father” or “dwelling of the father,” and of him the Scripture records nothing beyond his place in the order. The dictionary does not feign a history where the LORD was pleased to leave only a name and a number; it honours that the Spirit of God set down the head of the fourteenth course among the rest, that the worship of the sanctuary might be carried on decently and in order, without confusion. The lot was the LORD’s own way of settling the courses, that no priest might thrust himself before his brother nor any be wrongfully passed by. Jeshebeab, whose name speaks of a dwelling, served in his appointed week as a minister in the house of his God, where the LORD was pleased to dwell among His people. He stands as a witness that God is not the author of confusion but of order, and that the priests who ministered in the dwelling of the LORD were but servants in a house whose builder and maker is God; for the tabernacle of the old covenant pointed to the true dwelling, even Christ, in whom His people are built together for an habitation of God through the Spirit.

corruption_paragraphs: Jeshebeab is a name of the sacred record of the courses, and no movement of the present age has troubled itself to redefine it. The dictionary records it that the reader who meets the name at the head of the fourteenth course may know it for a real priest in a real order, set by a real God to minister in the house where He was pleased to dwell.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God ordereth His worship without confusion, and that the priests served in the dwelling of the LORD. He whose name in Jeshebeab speaks of a dwelling ministered in a house whose builder and maker is God. The saint who serves in the LORD’s house may remember Jeshebeab, named but once, and rejoice that he is builded together with the saints for an habitation of God through the Spirit, in Christ the true dwelling.

etymology: Hebrew bilgah, “cheerfulness” or “brightness,” the head of the fifteenth of the four and twenty courses of the priests appointed by David.
biblical_def: Bilgah is named as the head of the fifteenth course of the priests, the chief to whom the fifteenth lot came forth when David divided the sons of Aaron into their courses for the service of the house of God (1Ch 24:14). His name signifies “cheerfulness” or “brightness,” and his course endured beyond the captivity, for Bilgah is reckoned among the priests that went up with Zerubbabel and Jeshua, and among the heads of the priests in the days of Joiakim (Neh 12:5,18). Thus the order appointed under David was honoured again in the second house, a witness that the LORD preserved His worship and His servants through the long judgment of the exile and the joy of the return. The dictionary honours that the worship of God is to be carried on not in heaviness but in holy gladness, for the name of this course bespeaketh cheerfulness, and the LORD loveth a cheerful giver and a glad obedience. The casting of the lot ordered the courses in peace, that each might serve in his week with a willing heart. Bilgah stands as a witness that God is not the author of confusion but of order, and that the ordered worship of the old covenant, kept through captivity and restored with rejoicing, was a shadow of that better worship which the great High Priest hath opened, wherein His people draw near with boldness and serve the living God with joy.
